transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-04-10
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Sasha Martinez (Redwood AE), Ravi Patel (Redwood SE), Elena Cho (Redwood CSM), Jenna Lowe (HelioMed IT Lead), Mark O'Neil (ML Platform), Priya Gupta (Security), Carlos Ruiz (SRE), Tom Becker (Procurement)

Optional auto sections:
Topics: artifact delivery, offline licensing, GPU drivers, KV cache, batching, quantization, air-gapped install process, validation plan
Action items: see metadata

Transcript:
[00:00] Sasha Martinez: hey everyone thanks for joining on time um this is sasha from redwood inference, and today our goal is to walk through the on-prem air-gapped artifact delivery and offline licensing flow, plus cover driver compatibility and any runtime performance impacts. ravi will lead the technical pieces.
[00:10] Jenna Lowe: thanks sasha, appreciate it. we've got our infra folks here, mark and carlos, plus priya for security checks and tom for procurement background. we've got a pretty strict air-gap policy so want to make sure we capture all constraints.
[00:20] Ravi Patel: cool. quick agenda: artifact packaging and checksums, offline license activation, GPU driver compatibility and offline install, runtime runtime considerations - kv cache, batching, quantization settings that matter for onprem, and then a proposed validation plan. we'll pause for Qs as we go. sound good?
[00:35] Mark O'Neil: yep sounds good. our inventory: we've got a mix of A100 40GB, A100 80GB, and a small set of H100s in a segregated rack. air-gap means no outbound internet from the cluster, we use a jump box for one-way transfers.
[00:50] Ravi Patel: perfect. first, artifact delivery. we provide a signed tarball that contains: the runtime binary, model artifacts (if requested), container images as OCI tarballs, a driver bundle (optional), and an offline license token. the tarball is signed with our GPG key and we also provide SHA256 checksums and a detached signature file.
[01:10] Carlos Ruiz: how do we get that onto the cluster? our process is import via usb or via a transfer host that has an approved inbound from your secure ftp. we cannot pull.
[01:20] Sasha Martinez: we support both. two options: 1) we push to a secure SFTP endpoint; you download the artifacts from the SFTP to your jumpbox and then import to the cluster; 2) we provide the tarball through a signed physical media workflow - we can also coordinate an encrypted USB delivery if legal approves. both include checksums and a verification guide.
[01:35] Priya Gupta: important for us is reproducible verification. what metadata do you include? we need build hashes, container image digests, the gpg public fingerprint, and an SBOM.
[01:45] Ravi Patel: yes, we include build metadata.json (build id, date, commit hash), SBOM in SPDX format, image digests, and the GPG fingerprint. Note: transcription note, SBOM may sometimes show slightly different component names in older runtime builds.
[02:00] Jenna Lowe: good. offline licensing - how does activation work without outbound connectivity?
[02:05] Ravi Patel: offline licensing flow: we generate a customer-specific license blob tied to a cluster fingerprint. options: 1) you generate a signing request (CSR-style) on the jumpbox, transfer to us via SFTP, we sign and return a license token that you install locally; 2) if policy doesn't allow outbound, we can provide a time-limited license pre-generated for the cluster ID you supply in advance. tokens are encrypted and include expiry and entitlements (models allowed, node count).
[02:30] Tom Becker: procurement question - is there a paper license and an offline license key? how do we track node counts for billing?
[02:35] Elena Cho: on the commercial side, we provide a paper agreement and the offline license key. billing for Dedicated/Private is based on contract SKUs; for license enforcement we support node-count checks during runtime heartbeat but we can adapt to your preferred offline audit process - we can do periodic signed usage reports you upload.
[02:55] Priya Gupta: encryption and key management - where are keys stored? do you support HSM/KMS integration in an air-gapped mode?
[03:05] Ravi Patel: runtime supports customer-managed keys. in air-gapped mode we support on-prem KMS appliances or HSMs; the offline license decrypts with the local key. we will provide instructions for integrating with your HSM, and for customers without an HSM, keys can be stored in the node's secure keystore gated by OS-level protections.
[03:25] Carlos Ruiz: driver bundling - we run a locked-down baseline LTS kernel, and we prefer to manage driver installs ourselves. will you provide driver packages or do we need to pull from NVIDIA?
[03:35] Ravi Patel: we provide two choices: 1) a Redwood-validated driver bundle that we've tested with the runtime (we include the exact driver rpm/deb and installation scripts), or 2) a driver-agnostic install where we provide the runtime and a driver compatibility matrix - then you install vendor drivers yourself. For air-gapped customers with strict controls we typically deliver the validator bundle plus an offline verification test suite.
[03:55] Mark O'Neil: compatibility matrix - does it include CUDA versions, driver build IDs, and NCCL/UCX compat? we need to ensure network fabrics (InfiniBand) compatibility too.
[04:05] Ravi Patel: yes, matrix includes tested CUDA toolkit version, driver version, supported NCCL/UCX versions, and known fabric caveats. note: UCX settings can impact KV cache and batching performance; we document recommended UCX env vars.
[04:20] Jenna Lowe: any licensing implications for GPU vendor drivers? some vendors require separate offline license keys for enterprise drivers.
[04:25] Sasha Martinez: good point - GPU vendor drivers/licensing are separate. we can coordinate with your procurement to confirm whether driver binaries require separate licensing. our driver bundle can omit vendor-proprietary bits if needed, and we'll annotate which parts are vendor-supplied.
[04:40] Priya Gupta: runtime performance - we need to understand latency and throughput tradeoffs when running in our environment. slower NICs and constrained I/O might change batching behavior.
[04:50] Ravi Patel: yes. a few points: KV cache reduces redundant compute but consumes memory; we recommend allocating dedicated GPU memory for KV when latency SLO is strict. batching increases throughput but increases tail latency; our runtime supports adaptive batching with per-route SLOs. quantization reduces memory and bandwidth but may change inference quality - we provide quantization profiles (INT8/4-bit) with accuracy regressions in the SBOM so you can choose.
[05:15] Carlos Ruiz: with A100 40GB vs 80GB, any config differences?
[05:20] Ravi Patel: mainly KV allocation and model shard choices. on 80GB you can host larger KV caches and larger context windows without spilling to CPU; on 40GB you may need to use quantized model variants or smaller batch sizes to avoid OOM. we'll include recommended confs per SKU in the delivery notes.
[05:35] Mark O'Neil: what about multi-node serving and network overhead for KV sync?
[05:40] Ravi Patel: Redwood's default is local KV per-node with prefix routing to keep hot prefixes local. for highly stateful workloads we support a KV sync service that runs over your private fabric - for air-gapped installs it runs within the cluster. UCX/NCCL tuning is important; we'll supply UCX config suggestions and a small loadtest harness to validate.
[05:55] Jenna Lowe: can you walk through the offline validation plan?
[06:00] Ravi Patel: brief plan: 1) we deliver package + checksum, you verify signatures; 2) install drivers (either your vendor drivers or our bundle) on a staging node; 3) install runtime and license token; 4) run our smoke tests (startup, small inference, kv warmup); 5) run throughput/latency benchmarks we provide and collect logs; 6) we review results together. we'll provide scripts that produce an artifact (bench report + logs) you can upload to SFTP for us to look at.
[06:25] Priya Gupta: logs may contain sensitive info - can you sanitize or provide an option to strip prompts and user data before we send?
[06:30] Ravi Patel: yes, smoke/benchmark scripts have a redact mode that strips prompt text and returns only perf counters and file hashes. we'll document that.
[06:40] Tom Becker: procurement timelines - how long from order to artifact delivery?
[06:45] Sasha Martinez: typical lead time is 5-10 business days for a standard bundle once we have cluster fingerprint and signed agreement; custom driver bundles or HSM integrations may add time. we'll supply a timeline in the delivery email.
[06:55] Carlos Ruiz: offline install scripts - do you support orchestration with our existing config mgmt (ansible/chef) or only manual steps?
[07:00] Ravi Patel: we provide both: manual install docs and ansible playbooks that work in air-gapped mode. playbooks are parameterized for your hostnames and file paths.
[07:10] Jenna Lowe: one more question on quantization: do you provide per-workload evals showing quality delta vs full-fp32?
[07:15] Ravi Patel: yes, for major models we provide eval reports and recommended quant profiles. small regressions are expected on 4-bit in some benchmarks; we recommend integration tests with your prompt sets. we'll share example eval harness and instructions to run it offline.
[07:35] Priya Gupta: for compliance - do you generate audit logs for license activation and runtime start/stops?
[07:40] Elena Cho: yes, runtime generates signed audit logs for license events, model loads, and admin actions. logs can be configured to ship to your internal SIEM or kept locally per retention policy.
[07:50] Mark O'Neil: can the runtime operate without a license in read-only or degraded mode for emergency debugging?
[07:55] Ravi Patel: we support a short grace window for troubleshooting, but we generally require a valid offline license for production. emergency access is handled via time-limited debug tokens that must be requested via the secure channel; we can document that flow.
[08:10] Sasha Martinez: ok quick recap: we'll provide signed artifact tarball, SBOM, GPG fingerprint, driver bundle and/or compatibility matrix, offline license options (CSR or pre-generated), ansible playbooks, smoke and perf harness with redact mode, and a validation plan. action items are in the notes - ravi will produce driver checklist and install guide, sasha will send delivery instructions and timeline, jenny will return gpu sku inventory.
[08:40] Jenna Lowe: sounds good, thanks. one request - please include a short checklist for security to review before we accept physical media.
[08:45] Priya Gupta: yes include hash verification steps and what to look for in SBOM.
[08:50] Ravi Patel: will do.
[08:55] Sasha Martinez: ok thanks everyone, we'll follow up via the deal thread and set up the validation call for next week. bye.

End transcript.
